title: Think First, Then Ask AI
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Field Notes post warns that leaders who consult AI before forming their own view let its answer become the frame for their thinking. It cites an experiment with 240 teachers in training in which those who wrote their answers first handled flawed AI advice correctly 54 percent of the time, against 37 percent for those who asked AI first, plus similar findings in mock criminal cases and medication prescribing. Because most leadership work has no single right answer, the effect is hard to see: a first-draft strategy memo from AI quietly brings dozens of choices the leader might not have made. The fix is to write down an initial position, including what evidence would change it, and then use AI to develop that frame or to challenge it with prompts like 'What am I missing?' The post adds a caution that the goal is to hold a view, not defend it.
points: Asking AI first sets the frame for the whole decision, and leaders then judge every other option against it.
Experimental evidence across teaching, legal and medical settings shows worse judgment when faulty AI advice arrives before the person's own view.
Writing down an initial position and the evidence that would change it is the simple protective habit.
Prompts that challenge the frame, such as asking for the strongest case against it, make AI serve judgment instead of replacing it.
Thinking first is not a reason to dismiss good advice; a gap between your answer and the AI's is a cue to explore further.
quotes: When leaders and decision-makers ask AI before they have formed their own view, its answer becomes the frame for their thinking, and they judge every other option against it.

When the advice was flawed, those who wrote down their answer first got it right 54% of the time. Those who consulted AI first got it right only 37% of the time, and they repeated the bad advice nearly twice as often.
Most leadership work has no single right answer, which makes the effect harder to see. When leaders ask AI for a first draft of a strategy memo, the odds are high that they will keep its structure.
Under time pressure, the easier path is to accept the frame and polish what is inside it. Experience offers little protection.

Before leaders open AI, they would be best served by thinking through the issue on their own. Writing down an initial position, including what outcome is important and what evidence would change that view, helps to prevent this effect.
Prompts such as “What am I missing?” or “Make the strongest case against this” put AI to work for the leader’s judgment rather than in place of it.
The goal is to hold a view, not to defend it. When their own answer and the AI’s differ, good leaders treat the gap as a reason to explore more.
Thinking first and then asking AI keeps leaders in charge of their decisions and puts their judgment at the forefront, where it belongs.
